title: After-Hours Pager Response
scenario: It is 11:42 PM on a Saturday. Your pager goes off with an automated alert from the school monitoring system: the secondary internet circuit is down and the primary circuit is at 92% utilization. The alert severity is P1 because the school relies on remote access for the upcoming standardized testing window and the SIS nightly sync is at risk.
impact: Operational: if the primary circuit also fails, the school loses all internet, the SIS nightly sync will fail, and remote testing access will be unavailable. A two-circuit outage is a major incident.
objectives: Acknowledge the pager within the on-call response SLA
Assess scope and severity from the monitoring data
Open a major incident ticket if scope warrants it
Engage the ISP and the network vendor for the secondary circuit
Keep the CIO and on-call leadership informed
Document the response, the resolution, and any lessons learned

evidence.description: Network monitoring snapshot at time of alert: primary utilization, secondary status, latency
ISP support ticket number and the technician ETA
Timeline of actions taken during the on-call response and final resolution

decisionPoints.prompt: The pager went off at 11:42 PM. The on-call response SLA is 15 minutes. What is the right first action?

options.label: Open the monitoring dashboard remotely and check the alert context before calling anyone
options.feedback: You can do this, but the SLA requires acknowledging the page first. Acknowledge, then investigate.

options.label: Acknowledge the page within the SLA, then open the monitoring dashboard to investigate
options.feedback: Correct — acknowledge first to stop the escalation timer, then investigate the alert with full attention.

options.label: Defer the page to the morning — the primary circuit is still up
options.feedback: Deferring a P1 with the secondary already down is a gamble you will not win. Acknowledge and act now.

decisionPoints.prompt: The monitoring dashboard confirms: secondary circuit is down, primary at 92% and climbing. SIS nightly sync is scheduled for 2:00 AM. Should you declare a major incident?

options.label: Yes — declare a major incident, open the bridge, and engage the CIO and network vendor
options.feedback: Correct — single-circuit operation with a critical scheduled job is a P1. Declare MI, open the bridge, and engage stakeholders.

options.label: Wait and see — the primary might stabilize on its own
options.feedback: Waiting until the primary fails leaves no time to recover. Declare MI now and gain the response time.

options.label: Skip the SIS nightly sync to reduce primary load and wait until morning
options.feedback: Skipping the sync without authorization will create data integrity issues. Pause the sync only with CIO approval and a plan to resume.

ticket.initialDescription: Pager alert at 23:42: secondary internet circuit down. Primary circuit at 92% utilization and rising. SIS nightly sync at 02:00. Standardized testing window opens Monday.

nodes.title: Receive the page
nodes.body: Your pager just went off at 11:42 PM Saturday. The alert is P1. Note the on-call response SLA: acknowledge within 15 minutes. Take a breath and act, do not react.

nodes.title: Acknowledge the page
nodes.body: Choose the right first action when a P1 page arrives after hours.

nodes.title: Investigate the alert
nodes.body: Open the monitoring dashboard remotely. Capture the circuit statuses, utilization, and the scheduled SIS sync time. Save the monitoring snapshot as evidence.

nodes.title: Decide on major incident
nodes.body: Secondary down, primary at 92% and climbing, SIS sync at 02:00. Should you declare a major incident?

nodes.title: Engage ISP and notify CIO
nodes.body: Open the ISP support ticket. Get a technician ETA. Notify the CIO via phone (not email). Open the major incident bridge. Save the ISP ticket and the CIO notification as evidence.

nodes.title: Monitor and decide on the sync
nodes.body: Monitor the primary circuit utilization. With CIO approval, decide whether to pause the 02:00 SIS sync or let it run. Document the decision and the rationale.

nodes.title: Validate the recovery
nodes.body: Confirm the secondary circuit is restored and primary utilization has dropped. Validate the SIS sync outcome. Capture the resolution timeline and save as evidence.

nodes.title: Document the on-call response
nodes.body: Write the on-call incident log: page time, acknowledgement time, investigation, ISP engagement, sync decision, resolution time, and lessons learned. Send the summary to the CIO and the on-call rotation lead by morning.
nodes.prompt: Write the on-call incident summary for the CIO: timeline, decisions, resolution, and any follow-up actions for the network team.

nodes.title: Debrief
nodes.body: Review the on-call response. Key lessons: acknowledge within the SLA, declare a major incident when the impact warrants it, engage the ISP and CIO early, and document everything while it is fresh.

kbOpportunity: After-hours on-call response: acknowledge within SLA → investigate monitoring data → declare major incident if warranted → engage ISP and notify CIO → make authorized decisions on scheduled jobs → validate and document while fresh.
